title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (2 of 7)
hook: the second half of the first verse, and a question: whose is it?
tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (3 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: renounce and enjoy, the first half. All this, whatever moves, is pervaded by the Lord. Did you look at one ordinary thing as if it were lived in? Day two hundred thirty-three.
screen: `ALL THIS IS PERVADED BY THE LORD.`

segments.voice: A book lent to a friend can do something odd. While it's gone, its owner may think about it more than when it sat on the shelf. When it comes back, it gets noticed again. There's a strange thing about holding: the tighter the grip, the less there is to taste. A hand busy guarding can't do much else. The Isha Upanishad's first verse has a second half, and it turns on exactly this. Three short phrases. One instruction, one warning, and a question that sounds almost rude.
screen: `THE BOOK LENT TO A FRIEND.` → `GUARDING IS NOT TASTING.` → `THE SECOND HALF.`

segments.voice: Here's the second half. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha. By that renounced, enjoy. Or, as it's often put: enjoy through renunciation. Tyakta is let go, given up. Bhunjitha is enjoy, eat, have the use of. They sit side by side, which is the surprise. You might expect a holy text to say: renounce, so you won't enjoy. This one says the letting go is the way you get to enjoy. Why? Go back to yesterday. If all this belongs to the Lord, then you were never the owner. You're a guest at a table someone else set. A guest who grabs the dishes and hides them under the chair doesn't enjoy dinner. A guest who knows it's all a gift can eat with both hands. The next phrase is the warning: ma gridhah. Do not covet. Don't grasp at more. And then the question: kasya svid dhanam? Whose, indeed, is wealth? Commentators read it two ways. Don't covet anyone's wealth, because it isn't really theirs either. Or, more pointed: whose is it, really? The answer the verse has already given is: the Lord's. Renouncing here doesn't have to mean leaving home or giving everything away, though some people in the tradition do exactly that. For a householder, some teachers, Gandhi among them, say it means holding things as a trustee, not a proprietor. Use them. Love them. Let them go when they go.
screen: `BY THAT RENOUNCED, ENJOY.` · `A GUEST AT A TABLE SET BY ANOTHER.` · `DO NOT COVET.` · `WHOSE IS WEALTH?` · then, large: `RENOUNCE AND ENJOY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Hold something in your hand: your phone, a cup, a pen. Feel its weight. Now say to yourself, not mine, lent. Keep holding it. Notice whether it feels any different. Then set it down, open your hands on your knees, and breathe. Let each breath be something you receive and give back. In, received. Out, returned. The bell holds the time.
Renounce and enjoy. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha: by that renounced, enjoy. Don't covet. Whose is wealth?
Your line: renounce, and enjoy. Today, pick one thing you own and use it like a guest would: with thanks, without gripping. Day two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers read 'tena tyaktena bhunjitha' as a rule for householders: live fully in the world, holding possessions as a trust rather than as one's own.

match.prompt: the second half of verse one — tap the pairs.

myth: the verse says renounce so that you won't enjoy
it says enjoy by renouncing: tena tyaktena bhunjitha.
the verse ends with a question
kasya svid dhanam: whose, indeed, is wealth?

fork.setup: all this belongs to the Lord. you're handed a good meal. what does the verse say?
options: refuse it: enjoyment is the problem.
enjoy it, having let go of owning it.
save it for later so no one else takes it.
fork.reveal: by that renounced, enjoy. the letting go is the way to taste it, not the end of tasting.

original.note: Sanskrit: tyaktena, by what is let go; from tyaj, to give up, the root of tyaga, renunciation.

trapdoor: what you thought: renounce means give it all up and suffer.
what it means: hold everything as belonging to the Lord, and then enjoy it.
what a scholar hears: tena tyaktena bhunjitha, ma gridhah kasya svid dhanam; commentators split on whether the question means 'whose?' or warns off another's wealth.
